Learning Objective
By the end of this worksheet, you will be able to:

Calculate and compare crude (overall) rates of success.
Identify a potential confounding variable from a problem description.
Perform a stratified analysis to calculate group-specific rates.
Explain how confounding can lead to Simpson’s Paradox, where group-specific trends are reversed in the aggregate data.

Step-by-Step Scaffolding Tasks

Step 1: The Naive (Overall) Comparison
First, let’s look at the data from a purely associational perspective, ignoring any other factors.

Task 1a: Calculate the overall success rate for patients who received Treatment A.

Guiding Question: What is the total number of patients who had a success with Treatment A? What is the total number of patients who received Treatment A?
Calculation: (Number of Successes for A) / (Total Number receiving A) = ?

Task 1b: Calculate the overall success rate for patients who received Treatment B.

Calculation: (Number of Successes for B) / (Total Number receiving B) = ?

Task 1c: Based only on these overall rates, which treatment appears to be more effective?




Step 2: Identifying a Potential Confounder
In our lecture, we discussed that observational comparisons can be misleading. A key piece of information was left out of the table above: doctors tend to assign the more invasive Treatment A to patients with large kidney stones, while patients with small stones often receive the standard Treatment B. Stone size is also known to affect the difficulty of the treatment.

Task 2a: In this scenario, what is the third variable that might be related to both the treatment assigned and the treatment’s success? This is our potential confounder.
Task 2b: Explain why this variable could be a confounder.

Guiding Question: How might stone size influence a doctor’s choice of treatment? How might stone size independently influence whether a treatment is successful?

title: How to Write a Great Critique
text:
Welcome to the central guide for your weekly paper critiques. The goal of this assignment is to train you not just to understand a paper, but to deconstruct its argument, question its assumptions, and situate it within the broader field of causal inference.
Our course uses a unique mix of readings: foundational methodological papers, applied case studies, and modern textbook chapters. Your critique assignment asks you to focus on the foundational paper for each week, but the key to an excellent critique is to skillfully synthesize insights from all three sources.


Depending on the paper, you will need to wear one of two hats: the theoretician’s hat for methodological papers or the peer reviewer’s hat for case studies.


(Applies to papers like Rubin 1974, Pearl 1995, Rosenbaum & Rubin 1983)
When a paper proposes a method, your critique should focus on the validity, logic, and impact of that method. Since there is no data analysis, you must analyze the abstract argument.
Use this four-step process to structure your thinking:

Deconstruct the Problem & Proposed Solution:

The Problem: What specific challenge in causal inference is the paper trying to solve? (e.g., How can we control for many confounders at once? How do we define a causal effect?)
The Solution: What is the paper’s core contribution? Explain the new concept (e.g., potential outcomes, propensity scores, DAGs) in your own words.

Analyze the Logic & Identification Strategy:

The “Why”: What is the central logical argument for why their solution works? Explain the intuition behind any theorems or proofs. (e.g., The authors prove the propensity score is a balancing score, meaning…)
The Assumptions: What are the precise assumptions needed for this logic to hold? (e.g., This entire framework rests on the untestable assumption of strong ignorability…)

Scrutinize the Assumptions & Plausibility:

Real-World Plausibility: In what kinds of real-world studies would these assumptions be plausible? Where would they likely fail? Use examples from the case study or your own knowledge.
Failure Modes: What are the practical limitations of the method? (e.g., The method offers no protection against unmeasured confounding and is sensitive to violations of the positivity assumption.)

Evaluate the Impact & Legacy:

The Impact: How did this paper change the field? What did it make possible?
The Legacy: What subsequent research or methods did it inspire? What is its biggest remaining limitation?





(Applies to papers like Yusuf et al. 1991, Snowden et al. 2011, and all of the “Expedition” readings)
When a paper makes a causal claim about the world using data, your critique should focus on the credibility of that claim. Your job is to act as a rigorous, skeptical peer reviewer.

Scrutinize the Causal Question & Design:

The Question: Is the causal question well-defined (PICO)? Is the target trial clear?
The Data: Is the data source appropriate? Are there risks of major measurement error?

Interrogate the Identification Strategy:

The DAG: Draw a DAG for this specific study, reflecting its variables and context.
Attack the Key Assumption: This is the core of your critique. Is the central assumption (e.g., unconfoundedness, parallel trends, exclusion restriction) plausible in this specific context? What unmeasured confounder or alternative explanation did the authors likely miss?

Audit the Diagnostics & Analysis:

The Diagnostics: Did the authors perform and show the essential diagnostic checks for their method? (e.g., balance plots for propensity scores; first-stage F-statistic for IV).
The Model: Was the statistical model appropriate for the outcome and data structure?

Challenge the Interpretation & Conclusion:

The Interpretation: Do the authors overstate their claims? Do they acknowledge their key limitations?
The Sensitivity Analysis: Did they quantify how robust their finding is to unmeasured confounding (e.g., with an E-value)? If not, it is a major weakness.
The Generalizability: Do they correctly interpret the scope of their finding (e.g., acknowledging a LATE is not an ATE)?






Your assignment is to critique the foundational paper. You will use the other readings to become a smarter critic.
Your Task: Critique Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), “The central role of the propensity score…”

Start with the Map (Textbook): You read Hernán & Robins, Chapter 12. You now have a modern understanding of propensity scores, the ATE, and balancing diagnostics.
Critique the Journal (Foundational Paper): You apply the “How to Critique a Foundational Paper” framework to Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983).

Problem: The paper addresses the problem of controlling for many confounders in observational studies.
Solution: It introduces the propensity score as a single-number summary for balancing covariates.
Logic: It proves the balancing property of the score.
Assumption: The entire method relies on the assumption of strong ignorability (unconfoundedness).

Enrich with the Expedition (Case Study): Now, you use Dehejia & Wahba (1999) to add depth to your critique.

In your section on Assumption Plausibility, you write: “Rosenbaum & Rubin’s framework is entirely dependent on the unconfoundedness assumption. The Dehejia & Wahba (1999) case study provides an ideal scenario where this assumption is arguably plausible. By using a rich administrative dataset with detailed pre-treatment earnings and employment histories, they were able to control for the most likely determinants of both entering the training program and future earnings.”
In your section on Impact & Legacy, you write: “A key limitation of the original paper is its focus on theory, with little guidance on diagnostics. The profound impact of this work is demonstrated in applications like Dehejia & Wahba, which established the now-standard practice of reporting standardized mean differences in a balance plot to empirically verify that the propensity score did, in fact, balance the observed covariates.”


By following this process, you are not critiquing the case study; you are using it as evidence to make your critique of the foundational paper more concrete, critical, and insightful.

This rubric outlines the criteria for evaluating your project proposal. The proposal is graded out of 50 points and accounts for 10% of your final course grade. The goal of this deliverable is to ensure that you have a well-defined, feasible, and causally-grounded research plan.

Causal Question & Motivation
10 pts
The causal question is specific, clear, and unambiguous. The motivation is compelling, grounded in public health/scientific relevance, and supported by appropriate citations.
The question is causal but could be more specific. The motivation is present but may be overly broad or not well-supported.

Causal Model (DAG)
15 pts
The DAG is plausible, clearly drawn, and includes the key exposure, outcome, and confounders. The justification for the DAG’s structure is thoughtful and demonstrates a strong understanding of the topic.

The DAG is missing, illegible, or fundamentally incorrect (e.g., contains cycles, reverses obvious causal pathways).


Target Trial Protocol
10 pts
The key components of the target trial (eligibility, treatment strategies, outcome) are clearly and precisely defined, demonstrating a strong grasp of the emulation framework.

Proposed Method(s) & Feasibility
5 pts
The proposed causal method is appropriate for the question and data. The plan is feasible within the scope of the course, and potential challenges are acknowledged.
A causal method is proposed but may not be the most appropriate. The feasibility of the plan is questionable.
No causal method is proposed, or the proposed method is incorrect for the stated problem.

title: STAT 579: Final Project Proposal
text:
This document serves as the proposal for the STAT 579 final project. The goal is to provide a clear, concise, and feasible plan for your target trial emulation. Please replace the instructional text (in italics) with your own content. The final proposal should be approximately 2-3 pages.

1. The Causal Question

State your primary research question in a single, clear sentence. It must be a causal question (e.g., “What is the causal effect of X on Y?”) and not merely associational.



2. Scientific Background and Motivation

In 1-2 paragraphs, explain the public health or scientific relevance of your question. Why is this an important question to answer? What is already known on the topic? Briefly cite 2-3 key references that motivate your study.



3. Data Source

Identify the observational dataset you will use. Describe the source of the data (e.g., NHANES 2017-2018 cycle, MIMIC-IV v2.0). List the key variables you plan to use for your exposure (A), outcome (Y), and the primary confounders (L) you identified in your DAG.



4. Preliminary Causal Model (DAG)

Insert an image of your Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) here. The DAG should represent your current understanding of the causal relationships between the exposure, outcome, and key covariates. Below the image, provide a brief (1 paragraph) justification for the structure, explaining the most important causal pathways and confounding variables.



5. Target Trial Emulation Protocol

Briefly outline the key components of your target trial protocol. You can do this in a bulleted list. This does not need to be exhaustive at this stage, but it should be specific.

Eligibility Criteria: e.g., “Adults aged 40-75 with no prior history of CVD.”
Treatment Strategies: e.g., “Initiate a statin within 30 days of the index date” vs. “Do not initiate a statin.”
Outcome: e.g., “Incidence of myocardial infarction or stroke within 5 years of follow-up.”




6. Proposed Causal Method(s)

In one paragraph, state the primary causal method you intend to use to estimate the effect (e.g., propensity score weighting, g-computation). Briefly explain why this method is appropriate for your question and data structure. Mention any key diagnostics you plan to perform (e.g., covariate balance checks).

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
text:
Welcome to the data exploration hub for your final project. Finding the right dataset is arguably the most important step in a successful causal inference study. A good dataset doesn’t just have interesting variables; it must have the right structure to allow for the emulation of a target trial.
This page provides you with two things: a powerful tool for searching broadly and a curated list of datasets that are known to be well-suited for this kind of work.

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
section: The Go-To Tool: Google Dataset Search
text:
The Go-To Tool: Google Dataset Search
Think of this as Google Scholar, but for data. The Google Dataset Search engine indexes thousands of data repositories from around the world. It is the best place to start when you have a specific topic in mind.
Launch Google Dataset Search 

Tips for Effective Searching
When searching, use keywords that describe the structure of the data you need, not just the topic. Good causal inference requires data where time is well-defined.

Combine your topic (e.g., “cancer”, “education”, “air pollution”) with structural keywords like:
“longitudinal study”
“cohort study”
“prospective data”
“panel data”
“linked mortality data”

section: Curated Datasets for Target Trial Emulation
text:
Curated Datasets for Target Trial Emulation
Not all datasets are created equal. The best datasets for TTE are longitudinal cohort studies, where a group of people is enrolled at a baseline point in time and followed forward. This structure allows us to properly define eligibility, measure confounders before treatment, and follow individuals for the outcome.
Here are a few high-quality, publicly-available datasets that are exceptionally well-suited for your project.

Framingham Heart Study

Why it’s great for TTE: This is the archetypal prospective cohort study. A cohort of residents from Framingham, MA, was enrolled in 1948 and has been followed ever since. It contains detailed baseline measurements of potential confounders (e.g., smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure) and tracks cardiovascular outcomes over many decades. It’s a perfect dataset for emulating a trial of an intervention (e.g., lifestyle change, medication) on heart disease.
Access: Data is available to researchers through a proposal process. Visit the Framingham Heart Study Website.



MIMIC-IV (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care)

Why it’s great for TTE: This database of ICU admissions contains high-resolution, time-stamped data. This is critical because you can precisely define time zero (e.g., time of admission, time of a specific diagnosis). Treatments (medications, ventilators) and outcomes are all logged with precise timing, allowing you to emulate a trial of a clinical intervention in a critical care setting and avoid biases like immortal time bias.
Access: Requires completion of a human subjects research training course. Visit the MIMIC-IV Website.



Add Health (The National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health)

Why it’s great for TTE: This is a classic longitudinal cohort. A representative sample of U.S. adolescents was enrolled in 1994-95 and has been followed into adulthood. This is ideal for questions where the “treatment” occurs in adolescence (e.g., participation in sports, a specific educational program) and the outcome occurs in adulthood (e.g., income, health status). The baseline wave contains rich data on potential confounders (family background, school environment, etc.).
Access: Public-use data is readily available. Visit the Add Health Website.



NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey) with Linked Mortality Data

Why it’s great for TTE: By itself, NHANES is a series of cross-sectional surveys. However, participants can be linked to the National Death Index. This transforms the dataset into a prospective cohort study. You can use the rich survey data at baseline (diet, lab values, lifestyle) to define eligibility and measure confounders. You can then emulate a trial where the outcome is long-term mortality.
Access: Data is publicly available from the CDC. Visit the NHANES Website.

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
text:
✅ Checklist for Evaluating a Dataset
When you find a dataset that looks promising, use this checklist to assess its suitability for a Target Trial Emulation project.

Can you define a clear time zero? Is there a variable that marks the start of follow-up for all individuals (e.g., date of enrollment, date of diagnosis, start of the school year)?
Are confounders measured at or before time zero? The fundamental requirement for confounding control is that your covariates are measured before the treatment is assigned.
Is the exposure/treatment variable well-defined? Can you clearly determine who is “treated” and “untreated” based on the data?
Is the outcome measured after time zero? The dataset must have follow-up data to ascertain the outcome after the intervention.
Is the follow-up period long enough? Is there sufficient time between treatment and outcome for a causal effect to plausibly occur?

If you can answer “yes” to these questions, you likely have a strong candidate dataset for your project.

title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference
text:
Course Overview
This graduate-level seminar introduces the theory and application of causal inference, with a strong emphasis on biostatistical and epidemiological contexts. The course builds from conceptual foundations and core assumptions to modern estimation methods for causal effects, emphasizing target trial emulation as a unifying framework.
Key frameworks and tools include:

Potential Outcomes Framework & SUTVA
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
Propensity Scores, IPW, and Doubly Robust Methods
Instrumental Variables
Mediation Analysis (NDE/NIE)
Marginal Structural Models (MSMs)
Sensitivity Analysis


Instructor’s Approach
Causal inference is not just a toolbox—it’s a rigorous way of thinking about cause and effect. We will prioritize:

Precise causal questions (not just statistical associations).
Transparency of assumptions (via DAGs and formal notation).
Identification before estimation (thinking carefully about what is learnable from data).
Critical robustness assessment (sensitivity, replication, target trial framing).

title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Formulate and distinguish causal from associational questions.
Represent assumptions using DAGs and counterfactual notation.
Evaluate and apply key assumptions (SUTVA, exchangeability, positivity).
Implement modern causal inference methods (propensity scores, IPW, MSMs, IVs, G-computation).
Decompose effects via mediation analysis.
Conduct sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.
Frame observational studies as target trial emulations.
Critically evaluate causal claims in the literature.

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Timeline & Deliverables

Week 1–2: Causal Question Definition

Submit a 1–2 paragraph causal question relevant to biostatistics, epidemiology, or social/biomedical sciences.
Include justification of why the question is causal (not associational).

Week 3–4: Preliminary DAG

Provide a directed acyclic graph (using dagitty or ggdag).
State which paths must be blocked for identification.
Identify potential sources of bias (confounding, selection, measurement error).

Week 5–6: Identification Strategy

Explicitly state whether exchangeability, positivity, SUTVA, and consistency are plausible.
Describe your strategy: backdoor adjustment, IV, MSM, or mediation.

Week 9: Project Proposal (10% of course grade)

3–5 pages.
Elements:

Research question & target trial specification (eligibility, treatment strategies, follow-up, outcome).
DAG & assumptions.
Identification strategy.
Planned data source (public dataset, your own research, or simulation).
Anticipated challenges.


Weeks 10–13: Analysis

Implement at least one causal method (e.g., IPW, g-computation, IV, mediation, MSM).
Provide R code and output with clear interpretation.
Conduct diagnostics (balance checks, overlap, weak instrument tests, model fit).
Perform at least one sensitivity analysis (e.g., E-values, Rosenbaum bounds, tipr).

Week 14: Presentation (10%)

12–15 minutes, conference-style.
Emphasize assumptions, robustness, and substantive conclusions—not just technical detail.

Final Paper (25%) – Due Finals Week

~12–15 pages, structured as a research article:

Introduction: Causal question and motivation.
Target Trial Protocol: Eligibility, treatment, follow-up, outcome, causal estimand.
Assumptions & Identification: DAG, assumptions, strategy.
Methods: Data source, causal methods used, software.
Results: Estimates, sensitivity analyses, robustness checks.
Discussion: Interpretation, limitations, implications.
Appendix: R code (clean, annotated).

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Detailed Instructions

Step 1: Choosing a Question

Prefer health, social, or biomedical contexts (e.g., effect of smoking on lung cancer, impact of job training on income, role of diet on heart disease).
The question must be causal, not descriptive.

Bad: “What factors are associated with depression?”
Good: “What is the effect of exercise on reducing depression severity?”




Step 2: DAG Construction

Must use dagitty or ggdag.
Include confounders, colliders, mediators, and selection mechanisms.
Explicitly identify adjustment set(s) and whether positivity holds.



Step 3: Identification & Assumptions

Address the three pillars:

Exchangeability (unconfoundedness, or IV/exclusion restriction justification).
Positivity (overlap diagnostics, trimming if needed).
Consistency & SUTVA (intervention is well-defined).




Step 4: Method Implementation

Choose a method appropriate to your design:

Backdoor adjustment: matching, stratification, regression, IPW.
IV: LATE, 2SLS.
Mediation: NDE/NIE decomposition.
MSM: time-varying exposures.

Use R packages: MatchIt, WeightIt, ivreg, mediation, EValue, tipr.



Step 5: Sensitivity Analysis

Required to evaluate robustness. Options:

E-value.
Rosenbaum bounds.
Simulated confounding (tipr).




Step 6: Writing & Presentation

Clarity of assumptions is more important than fancy methods.
Discussion must explicitly state: “If assumption X fails, my estimate is biased because…”

The chosen statistical method (e.g., IPW, g-comp) is appropriate and correctly implemented. Details (e.g., PS model specification, diagnostics) are clear and well-documented.
The method is appropriate, but implementation details are sparse or diagnostics are incomplete.
The chosen statistical method is inappropriate for the question, or its implementation is incorrect.


Results
15 pts
Results are presented clearly and logically (e.g., Table 1, balance plots, effect estimates). Figures are well-labeled and easy to interpret. A relevant sensitivity analysis (e.g., E-value) is performed and reported correctly.
Key results are present but may be poorly organized or labeled. The sensitivity analysis is missing or misinterpreted.
Results are missing, incorrect, or presented in a confusing way. No attempt at sensitivity analysis.


Discussion & Conclusion
15 pts
Thoughtful interpretation of findings. Limitations are discussed with a deep focus on the key causal assumptions. Connects results back to the scientific literature and discusses implications.
Interpretation is plausible but superficial. Limitations are listed without a deep connection to the study’s causal validity.
Results are misinterpreted. Discussion of limitations is absent or irrelevant.


Overall Quality
5 pts
The paper is exceptionally well-written, professionally formatted, and easy to follow. The R code appendix is clean and reproducible.
The paper is generally well-written but may have minor errors in formatting, grammar, or clarity.
The paper is difficult to read due to major issues with writing, structure, or formatting.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
text:
Imagine we have a large electronic health record (EHR) dataset and we want to answer the question: “Does taking statins prevent cardiovascular disease (CVD)?”


A traditional approach might look like this:

Data First: Open the dataset. Identify a variable for “statin use” (e.g., statin_ever_used) and an outcome variable for “CVD.”
Model: Choose a regression model. Let’s use logistic regression: CVD ~ statin_ever_used + age + sex + diabetes.
Result: Fit the model. Look at the odds ratio for statin_ever_used. If it’s less than 1 and the p-value is significant, conclude that statins are protective.

This seems straightforward, but it is filled with hidden pitfalls. The causal question is vague, and the analysis is susceptible to numerous biases that are difficult to see without a more structured framework.



The TTE framework forces us to change our entire workflow.

Mindset Shift: We start with the question, not the data. Our first step is to design the ideal, hypothetical randomized controlled trial (RCT) we wish we could run to answer our question. This is our “target trial.” Only after we have a complete “protocol” for this ideal trial do we turn to the observational data and see how well we can emulate it.

This disciplined process makes our assumptions explicit and helps us proactively design an analysis that avoids common biases.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
section: Tutorial: Building the Target Trial Protocol
text:
Tutorial: Building the Target Trial Protocol
The protocol of any trial (real or hypothetical) has key components. Let’s define them for our statin/CVD question and contrast the TTE approach with the “just analyze” approach at each step.

1. Eligibility Criteria

The Question: Who would be eligible to enroll in our ideal trial?
“Just Analyze” Approach: This is often an afterthought. We might just use all patients in the dataset who don’t have missing values for our variables of interest.
TTE Approach: We must be explicit. For our statin trial, we might specify:

Inclusion: Patients aged 40-75.
Exclusion: Patients with a history of CVD at baseline (since we’re studying prevention). Patients without continuous health plan enrollment for the prior year (to ensure we have their baseline data).
Why it matters: Excluding prevalent users (those already on statins) and requiring a clean baseline period is crucial for avoiding selection bias and ensuring we are comparing apples to apples.




2. Treatment Strategies

The Question: What are the precise interventions we are comparing?
“Just Analyze” Approach: We might use a vague statin_ever_used variable. But what does this mean? Did they take one pill? Take it for 10 years? This ambiguity is a major source of error.
TTE Approach: We must specify the strategies precisely, as in a real trial.

Strategy 1: Initiate a statin (e.g., atorvastatin, simvastatin) at baseline.
Strategy 2: Do not initiate a statin at baseline.
Why it matters: This pushes us towards a “new-user” design, where we only include patients at the moment they become eligible to start the therapy. This is a powerful tool to prevent biases.




3. Assignment Procedure

The Question: How are individuals assigned to a treatment strategy?
“Just Analyze” Approach: The assignment is whatever happened in the real world. We hope to “control for confounding” by adding covariates to a regression model.
TTE Approach: In our ideal target trial, we would assign treatment randomly at baseline. In the real world, this is obviously not the case; doctors assign statins for reasons (confounding). Our task is to emulate randomization. We do this by adjusting for a sufficient set of baseline confounders (identified by our DAG!) using methods like:

Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW): Creating a “pseudo-population” where the confounders are no longer associated with treatment assignment.
Matching: Matching treated individuals to untreated individuals with similar baseline characteristics.
Why it matters: This makes the goal of “controlling for confounding” a deliberate design choice, not just a modeling exercise. We are explicitly trying to create groups that are exchangeable, just like in a real RCT.




4. Follow-up Period

The Question: When does follow-up begin and end?
“Just Analyze” Approach: The start of follow-up is often poorly defined. Does it start when the patient enters the database? Or when they first use a statin?
TTE Approach: The start of follow-up (time zero) must be the same for everyone: the moment of treatment assignment (or emulation of assignment).

For new users, this is the date of their first statin prescription.
For non-users, we can assign a similar “index date.”
Follow-up ends at a pre-specified time (e.g., 5 years), or when CVD occurs, or when they leave the health plan (censoring).
Why it matters: Properly defining time zero is the single most effective way to prevent immortal time bias. This bias occurs when a period of follow-up is misclassified as “unexposed” when it should be “not yet exposed,” leading to a spurious protective effect.




5. Outcome

The Question: How do we define the outcome?
TTE Approach: We need to specify the outcome just as we would in a trial protocol (e.g., “first diagnosis of a myocardial infarction or stroke, identified via ICD-10 codes during an inpatient hospital stay”). This clarity reduces measurement error.



6. Causal Contrasts (Estimand)

The Question: What is the precise causal effect we are trying to estimate?
“Just Analyze” Approach: This is often implicit in the model output (e.g., an odds ratio).
TTE Approach: We specify our estimand up front. The two main choices are:

Intention-to-Treat (ITT) effect: The effect of assigning the treatment strategy at baseline, regardless of whether the patient adheres to it later. This is often emulated in observational data.
Per-Protocol effect: The effect of adhering to the treatment strategy over time. This is more complex and requires advanced methods like Marginal Structural Models (MSMs) to handle time-varying confounding.
Why it matters: Being explicit about the estimand dictates the correct analysis plan and prevents misinterpretation of the results.




7. Analysis Plan

The Question: How will we estimate the causal contrast?
“Just Analyze” Approach: Fit a single regression model.
TTE Approach: The analysis plan flows directly from all the previous design choices. If emulating an ITT effect, we might use a weighted Cox model (using IPTW) that compares the two groups from time zero. If estimating a per-protocol effect, we would need to specify how we will handle treatment switching and censoring.

section: Summary: Why Target Trial Emulation is Different
text:
Summary: Why Target Trial Emulation is Different








Feature
“Just Analyzing Data”
Target Trial Emulation




Starting Point
The dataset and its variables
A precise causal question & an ideal trial protocol


Assumptions
Often implicit, hidden in the model
Explicitly stated in the protocol design


Bias Avoidance
Reactive (hope regression “controls” for it)
Proactive (design choices to prevent bias)


Transparency
Low; it’s hard to know exactly what was compared
High; the emulated protocol is the roadmap for the analysis


Rigor
Variable; prone to hidden errors
High; provides a systematic framework



In short, target trial emulation is not a statistical method. It’s a structured way of thinking. It’s the overarching framework that guides you to ask the right questions, design a sound observational analysis, choose the right statistical methods, and avoid preventable biases. It turns a simple data analysis into a credible scientific investigation.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
text:
Trial Emulation Example
Here are the seven components of a target trial designed to answer the question: “What is the effect of obtaining a bachelor’s degree on personal income?”

1. Eligibility Criteria
This defines the population for our hypothetical trial. We can’t include everyone. We need a specific cohort of people who are at the point of making the decision.

Eligible Population: All individuals who graduated from a U.S. high school in a specific year (e.g., 2010), are between 17-19 years old at graduation, and have not yet enrolled in a 4-year college program.
Exclusions: Individuals who are not eligible to apply to a 4-year college or who already possess an associate’s degree or other advanced vocational certification.



2. Treatment Strategies
These are the precise interventions we want to compare. “Getting a degree” is too vague.

Strategy 1 (Treated): Enroll in a 4-year bachelor’s degree program within one year of high school graduation and successfully obtain a bachelor’s degree within six years of high school graduation.
Strategy 2 (Control): Do not obtain a bachelor’s degree within six years of high school graduation. (This group may enter the workforce, attend community college, or pursue vocational training.)



3. Assignment Procedure
In an ideal world, we would randomize. In our emulation, we mimic that randomization.

Ideal Trial: Eligible individuals would be randomly assigned at high school graduation to either pursue the “degree” strategy or the “no degree” strategy.
Emulation: We use observational data and adjust for the baseline factors that influence both the decision to attend college and future income. This is our confounder set. We would use methods like propensity score weighting or matching to balance the two groups on key baseline variables measured at high school graduation, such as:

High School GPA and class rank
Standardized test scores (SAT/ACT)
Family income and socioeconomic status
Parental education level
High school quality and resources




4. Follow-up Period
This defines the timeline for our study, and time zero is critical.

Start of Follow-up (Time Zero): The clock starts for everyone at the same moment: right after high school graduation (e.g., September 1, 2010). This is the point of (emulated) randomization.
End of Follow-up: The follow-up period ends when the outcome is measured. A reasonable point would be 12 years after high school graduation, when individuals are approximately 30 years old and have had time to establish themselves in their careers.



5. Outcome
This is the specific event we are measuring.

Primary Outcome: Annual personal pre-tax income at age 30, measured in U.S. dollars. The data source (e.g., tax records, survey data) must be specified.



6. Causal Contrasts (Estimand)
This is the specific statistical quantity we aim to estimate.

Estimand: The Average Treatment Effect (ATE). Specifically, we want to calculate the difference in mean annual income at age 30 between the group assigned to Strategy 1 and the group assigned to Strategy 2. This is an “intention-to-treat” estimand, as it measures the effect of being assigned to a strategy at baseline, regardless of eventual adherence (e.g., some people assigned to the college track might drop out).



7. Analysis Plan
This outlines the statistical steps to estimate the causal contrast.

The Plan:

Among the eligible cohort of 2010 high school graduates, fit a model (e.g., logistic regression) to estimate each person’s probability of attending college based on the baseline confounders (GPA, family income, etc.). This yields the propensity score.
Use these propensity scores to calculate inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) to create a pseudo-population where the baseline confounders are balanced between the two groups.
In this weighted pseudo-population, calculate the mean income at age 30 in the group that obtained a degree and the group that did not.
The difference between these two means is the estimate of the causal effect. We would then calculate a 95% confidence interval around this estimate.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
text:
The goal when reading a methodological paper is not to memorize every formula but to build a robust mental model of the author’s argument. You want to understand the problem they solved, the logic of their solution, the assumptions required for it to work, and its ultimate impact. This active, model-building approach is far more effective than passive reading.
We will use a Three-Pass Approach designed to manage cognitive load and build your understanding from a scaffold to a fully-formed structure.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 1: The Bird’s-Eye View – Building the Scaffold (15 Minutes) 🗺️
text:
Pass 1: The Bird’s-Eye View – Building the Scaffold (15 Minutes) 🗺️
Don’t start by reading page one. Your first goal is to create a mental “map” of the paper’s purpose and structure. This provides a scaffold for your brain to hang the details on later, which significantly reduces cognitive load.

Read the Abstract, Introduction, and Conclusion First: Read these three sections carefully. At the end of this step, you should be able to answer, in simple terms:

The Problem: What specific challenge or gap in knowledge existed before this paper was written?
The Solution: What is the main idea, method, or framework this paper proposes?
The Claim: What do the authors claim is the primary impact or takeaway of their work?

Scan the Section Headings: Look at the structure of the paper. How do the authors build their argument from the problem to the solution?
Examine Figures and Conceptual Tables: Look at any diagrams (like DAGs), charts, or conceptual tables. Read their captions. These often contain the most important ideas in a condensed, visual format.

At the end of this pass, you shouldn’t understand the details, but you should have a clear sense of the paper’s story.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 2: The Deep Dive – Adding the Bricks with Active Recall (1-2 Hours) 🧱
text:
Pass 2: The Deep Dive – Adding the Bricks with Active Recall (1-2 Hours) 🧱
Now, read the paper from start to finish, but with an active, questioning mindset. Your goal is to deconstruct the argument, not just consume it.

“Translate” the Math: When you encounter a block of equations, your goal is not to re-derive the proofs. Instead, focus on the English sentences before and after the math. Your task is to translate the mathematical statement into a conceptual one. For example, when you see the formula for the propensity score, you should translate it in your notes as: “This is the probability of getting the treatment, given the measured covariates L.”
Focus on the Assumptions: For causal inference papers, assumptions are the most important part. They are the weak points of any argument. When an assumption is stated (e.g., “unconfoundedness,” “exclusion restriction”), stop and ask:

What does this assumption mean conceptually?
Why is it necessary for the author’s argument to work?
Is this assumption testable? If not, in what real-world scenarios might it be plausible or implausible?

Engage in Active Recall: After reading each major section, stop, look away from the page, and ask yourself: “What was the single most important point of that section?” Try to summarize it in one or two sentences, either in your head or in your notes. This act of forcing your brain to retrieve the information is far more powerful for learning than passively re-reading the text.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 3: The Feynman Technique – Solidifying Understanding (30 Minutes) ✍️
text:
Pass 3: The Feynman Technique – Solidifying Understanding (30 Minutes) ✍️
You only truly understand something when you can explain it simply. This final pass solidifies your mental model and reveals any remaining gaps in your knowledge.

Put the paper away. Open a blank document or grab a piece of paper.
Explain the paper to an imaginary first-year graduate student. Your explanation must clearly and simply answer the following five questions:

What was the central problem the authors were trying to solve?
What was their key insight or proposed solution?
In simple terms, what is the core logic for why their solution works?
What are the 1-3 critical assumptions it relies on to be valid?
What is the single biggest limitation or most important implication of this work?


If you get stuck or find yourself using jargon you can’t define, you’ve found the edge of your understanding. Go back to the paper and focus specifically on that part. This technique is the most efficient way to build deep, lasting comprehension.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Example Application: The Feynman Technique for Week 5 (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983)
text:
Example Application: The Feynman Technique for Week 5 (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983)
After reading the paper, your Feynman explanation might look like this:

Problem: In observational studies, people who get a treatment are different from those who don’t across many variables (confounders). Trying to adjust for all of them in a single regression model is complicated and non-transparent.
Solution: They proposed the propensity score—the probability of getting treated given your set of covariates. They proved you only need to adjust for this single number to remove bias from all observed confounders.
Logic: The propensity score has a “balancing property.” At any given value of the score, the distribution of the covariates is the same between the treated and untreated groups, just like in a randomized experiment.
Assumptions: This only works if you’ve measured all the important confounders (unconfoundedness) and if there are both treated and untreated people at every level of the propensity score (positivity/overlap). Unconfoundedness is a huge, untestable assumption.
Impact: This revolutionized observational research by creating a two-step process: first, focus on study design by creating balanced groups, and only then, perform the outcome analysis. Its biggest limitation is that it does nothing to solve the problem of unmeasured confounders.

title: Weekly Paper Critique Schedule
text:
Part I: Foundations

Week 1 – Causal Effects & SUTVA

Classic: Rubin, D. B. (1974). Estimating causal effects of treatments in randomized and nonrandomized studies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 66(5), 688–701. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0037350
Summary: Introduces the potential outcomes framework, defines causal effects as counterfactual contrasts, and articulates the “fundamental problem of causal inference.”
Questions:

In your own words, what is the fundamental problem of causal inference?

Why is the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) necessary? Give a real-world example of violation.

How does this framework clarify the difference between causal effects and observed associations?

Modern: Rubin, D. B. (2005). Causal inference using potential outcomes: Design, modeling, decisions. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 100(469), 322–331. https://doi.org/10.1198/016214504000001880
Summary: Reflects on the evolution of the framework, emphasizing “design trumps analysis” and transparency of assumptions.
Questions:

What does Rubin mean by “design trumps analysis”? Provide an example.

How does the framework make assumptions explicit compared to regression?

What challenges arise when prioritizing design in observational studies?




Week 2 – DAGs

Classic: Greenland, S., Pearl, J., & Robins, J. M. (1999). Causal diagrams for epidemiologic research. Epidemiology, 10(1), 37–48. https://doi.org/10.1097/00001648-199901000-00008
Summary: Introduces Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) as a language for representing causal assumptions and identifying confounding, colliders, and valid adjustment sets.
Questions:

Draw a DAG for your own research area, identifying one confounder, one mediator, and one collider.

What is the back-door criterion, and why does it justify covariate adjustment?

Why is conditioning on a collider problematic? Provide an example.

Modern: Textor, J., van der Zander, B., Gilthorpe, M. S., Liśkiewicz, M., & Ellison, G. T. H. (2016). Robust causal inference using directed acyclic graphs: The R package dagitty. International Journal of Epidemiology, 45(6), 1887–1894. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw341
Summary: Introduces dagitty, a tool to automate adjustment set selection, evaluate testable implications, and visualize DAGs.
Questions:

What are the advantages of using dagitty versus manual identification?

How do testable implications help assess a DAG?

What limitations remain in relying on software for causal modeling?




Week 3 – Exchangeability / Positivity / Consistency

Classic: Holland, P. W. (1986). Statistics and causal inference. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 81(396), 945–960. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1986.10478354
Summary: Clarifies Rubin’s model by distinguishing association vs. causation, stressing “no causation without manipulation,” and outlining assumptions of exchangeability, positivity, and consistency.
Questions:

How does “no causation without manipulation” distinguish causes from attributes?

What are the three core assumptions for causal inference?

Which assumption is hardest to verify in practice, and why?

Modern: Hernán, M. A. (2018). The C-word: Scientific euphemisms do not improve causal inference from observational data. American Journal of Public Health, 108(5), 616–619. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2018.304337
Summary: Critiques euphemisms like “associated with,” arguing that explicit causal language enforces clarity about assumptions.
Questions:

What risks arise from using causal euphemisms?

Do you agree with Hernán that researchers should always say “cause”? Why or why not?

When might it be valid to avoid causal language?


Perfect — let’s finish the Weekly Reading & Critique Hub with Weeks 4–13. I’ll present them in the same Quarto-ready format (summary + three questions per paper).


Week 4 – Confounding & Selection Bias

Classic: Hernán, M. A., Hernández-Díaz, S., & Robins, J. M. (2004). A structural approach to selection bias. Epidemiology, 15(5), 615–625. https://doi.org/10.1097/01.ede.0000135174.63482.43
Summary: Provides a unified framework for selection bias using DAGs, showing how many biases (Berkson’s bias, loss-to-follow-up) arise from conditioning on a collider.
Questions:

Draw a DAG illustrating how restricting to hospitalized patients induces spurious associations.

How can loss-to-follow-up be represented in a DAG, and under what conditions does it bias estimates?

Why is collider bias a unifying explanation for many selection biases?

Modern: Cole, S. R., & Hernán, M. A. (2002). Fallibility in estimating direct effects. International Journal of Epidemiology, 31(1), 163–165. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/31.1.163
Summary: Demonstrates via DAGs that adjusting for mediators with regression can misestimate direct effects if there is unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding.
Questions:

Why does the standard regression approach to mediation often fail?

How does unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding complicate direct effect estimation?

How does this set the stage for modern causal mediation analysis?

text:
Part II: Estimation Methods

Week 5 – Propensity Scores
(see prior section — already complete)


Week 6 – IPTW & Marginal Structural Models

Classic:
Robins, J. M., Hernán, M. A., & Brumback, B. (2000). Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology, 11(5), 550–560. https://doi.org/10.1097/00001648-200009000-00011

Why does standard regression fail when confounders are also mediators?

Week 7 – G-computation & TMLE

Classic: Robins, J. M. (1986). A new approach to causal inference in mortality studies with sustained exposure periods—application of the G-formula. Mathematical Modelling, 7(9–12), 1393–1512. https://doi.org/10.1016/0270-0255(86)90088-6

How does g-computation differ from IPTW?

What is sequential exchangeability, and why is it critical?

What are the pros/cons of outcome-modeling approaches?

Modern: Petersen, M. L., & van der Laan, M. J. (2014). Causal models and learning from data: Integrating causal modeling and statistical estimation. Epidemiology, 25(3), 418–426. https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000000078
Summary: Describes Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE), a doubly robust method combining causal models with efficient estimation.
Questions:

What does “doubly robust” mean in practice?

How does TMLE improve on g-computation?

Why separate identification from estimation in causal analysis?




Week 8 – Instrumental Variables

Classic: Angrist, J. D. (1990). Lifetime earnings and the Vietnam era draft lottery: Evidence from social security administrative records. American Economic Review, 80(3), 313–336. http://www.jstor.org/stable/2006669
Summary: Uses the Vietnam draft lottery as an instrument to estimate the causal effect of military service on earnings.
Questions:

What three assumptions must hold for a valid instrument?

Who are the “compliers,” and why does IV identify their effect?

Which IV assumption is least plausible here?

Modern: Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J.-S. (2010). The credibility revolution in empirical economics. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 24(2), 3–30. https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.24.2.3
Summary: Argues that modern applied economics has shifted to emphasize credible research designs (IV, RD, DiD).
Questions:

What is the “credibility revolution”?

How does design alter the role of modeling in causal inference?

What risks exist in over-reliance on quasi-experiments?

title: Weekly Paper Critique Schedule
text:
Part III: Advanced Topics

Week 9 – Effect Modification & Interaction

Classic:
Rothman, K. J. (1974). Synergy and antagonism in cause–effect relationships. American Journal of Epidemiology, 99(6), 385–388. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a121617
Summary: Introduces the sufficient-component cause (“causal pies”) model, framing synergy and antagonism among causes.
Questions:

How can two factors show additive but not multiplicative interaction?

How does the causal pie model explain effect heterogeneity?

Why is additive interaction often more relevant in public health?

Modern: VanderWeele, T. J. (2019). Principles of effect modification and interaction. International Journal of Epidemiology, 48(1), 301–308. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyy276
Summary: Clarifies interaction concepts, advocating for additive-scale measures and subgroup reporting.
Questions:

Why report subgroup-specific effects instead of only an interaction p-value?

Distinguish “effect modification” from “statistical interaction.”

How does effect modification inform policy?




Week 10 – Mediation I

Classic:
Baron, R. M., & Kenny, D. A. (1986). The moderator–mediator variable distinction in social psychological research. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 51(6), 1173–1182. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.51.6.1173
Summary: Proposes the traditional four-step regression-based framework for mediation.
Questions:

What are the four Baron–Kenny steps?

What hidden assumptions are needed for causal interpretation?

Why is this approach now considered insufficient?

Modern: Imai, K., Keele, L., & Tingley, D. (2010). A general approach to causal mediation analysis. Psychological Methods, 15(4), 309–334. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0020761
Summary: Develops a potential outcomes framework for mediation, defining natural direct/indirect effects under sequential ignorability.
Questions:

What is sequential ignorability, and why is it strong?

How do natural effects improve on Baron–Kenny?

What challenges arise in applying this approach?




Week 11 – Mediation II & Principal Stratification

Classic:
Robins, J. M., & Greenland, S. (1992). Identifiability and exchangeability for direct and indirect effects. Epidemiology, 3(2), 143–155. https://doi.org/10.1097/00001648-199203000-00013
Summary: Provides counterfactual definitions of direct/indirect effects, requiring sequential exchangeability and no exposure–mediator interaction.
Questions:

What are the two parts of sequential exchangeability?

Why does exposure–mediator interaction block nonparametric identification?

How does this extend mediation beyond Baron–Kenny?

Modern: Daniel, R. M., De Stavola, B. L., Cousens, S. N., & Vansteelandt, S. (2015). Causal mediation analysis with multiple mediators. Epidemiology, 26(3), 364–372. https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000000253
Summary: Extends mediation analysis to multiple, possibly correlated mediators, introducing assumptions for path-specific effects.
Questions:

Why can’t indirect effects from separate single-mediator models be summed?

What new assumptions are needed for path-specific effects?

How does this reflect real-world complexity?




Week 12 – Sensitivity Analysis

Classic:
Rosenbaum, P. R. (1987). Sensitivity analysis for matched observational studies. Biometrika, 74(1), 13–26. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/74.1.13
Summary: Introduces sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding in matched studies, quantifying how strong a hidden confounder must be to change conclusions.
Questions:

What is the key idea behind Rosenbaum’s sensitivity analysis?

Why is sensitivity analysis critical in observational causal studies?

How might this framework be adapted for non-matched designs?

Modern: VanderWeele, T. J., & Ding, P. (2017). Sensitivity analysis in observational research: Introducing the E-value. Annals of Internal Medicine, 167(4), 268–274. https://doi.org/10.7326/M16-2607
Summary: Proposes the E-value, a simple measure of how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away an observed association.
Questions:

How do you interpret an E-value of 3.0 for a risk ratio of 2.0?

What are the assumptions behind the E-value?

What are its limitations compared to full sensitivity analyses?




Week 13 – Target Trial Emulation

Classic: Robins, J. M. (1987). A graphical approach to the identification and estimation of causal parameters in mortality studies with sustained exposure periods. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 40(Suppl. 2), 139S–161S. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0021-9681(87)80033-0
Summary: Early graphical framework showing how observational data can emulate randomized trials with sequential treatments.
Questions:

Why emulate a randomized trial with observational data?

What is this paper’s key conceptual contribution?

How do DAGs/graphs assist in this setting?

Modern: Hernán, M. A., Alonso, A., Logan, R., Grodstein, F., Michels, K. B., Willett, W. C., Manson, J. E., & Robins, J. M. (2008). Specifying a target trial prevents immortal time bias and other self-inflicted injuries in observational analyses. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 61(1), 41–45. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2007.03.014
Summary: Outlines the target trial framework, showing how explicitly defining trial components prevents immortal time bias.
Questions:

What is immortal time bias, and how does a target trial prevent it?

What are the seven key components of a target trial protocol?

How does target trial emulation improve transparency?

Why Causality?

We ask: Does X cause Y?
Examples:

Does ☕ coffee cause longer life?

Does 📚 tutoring improve exam scores?

title: Introduction to Causal Inference & the Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
Potential Outcomes Framework
For each unit \(i\):

\(Y_i^{(1)}\): Outcome if treated

\(Y_i^{(0)}\): Outcome if not treated

Individual causal effect:
\[\tau_i = Y_i^{(1)} - Y_i^{(0)}\]

text:
Concept Check 1
Which statement is true?
A. We can always observe both \(Y^{(1)}\) and \(Y^{(0)}\).
B. The causal effect is \(Y^{(1)} + Y^{(0)}\).
C. The causal effect is the difference \(Y^{(1)} - Y^{(0)}\).
D. Potential outcomes are irrelevant.
👉 Discuss and vote.

The Fundamental Problem
⚠️ Only one potential outcome observed:
- If treated: observe \(Y^{(1)}\).
- If not treated: observe \(Y^{(0)}\).
This is the Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference.

Average Causal Effect (ACE)
We usually care about the population average:
\[ACE = \mathbb{E}[Y^{(1)} - Y^{(0)}]\]
But we cannot see both potential outcomes → need assumptions.

👉 Small group discussion.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference & the Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
Key Assumptions
1. SUTVA

Outcomes not affected by others’ treatment.
No hidden versions of treatment.

Example: My test score ≠ influenced by your tutoring.
Violation: Herd immunity in vaccines.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference & the Potential Outcomes Framework
text:

Interference: Peer effects in education (your study group matters).

Hidden versions: Drug dose differences, not accounted for.

title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference
text:
Course Overview
This graduate-level seminar introduces the theory and application of causal inference, with a strong emphasis on biostatistical and epidemiological contexts. The course builds from conceptual foundations and core assumptions to modern estimation methods for causal effects, emphasizing target trial emulation as a unifying framework.
Key frameworks and tools include:

Potential Outcomes Framework & SUTVA
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
Propensity Scores, IPW, and Doubly Robust Methods
Instrumental Variables
Mediation Analysis (NDE/NIE)
Marginal Structural Models (MSMs)
Sensitivity Analysis


Instructor’s Approach
Causal inference is not just a toolbox—it’s a rigorous way of thinking about cause and effect. We will prioritize:

Precise causal questions (not just statistical associations).
Transparency of assumptions (via DAGs and formal notation).
Identification before estimation (thinking carefully about what is learnable from data).
Critical robustness assessment (sensitivity, replication, target trial framing).

title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Formulate and distinguish causal from associational questions.
Represent assumptions using DAGs and counterfactual notation.
Evaluate and apply key assumptions (SUTVA, exchangeability, positivity).
Implement modern causal inference methods (propensity scores, IPW, MSMs, IVs, G-computation).
Decompose effects via mediation analysis.
Conduct sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.
Frame observational studies as target trial emulations.
Critically evaluate causal claims in the literature.
